segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying, and my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I could wish that I myself were accursed, cut off from Christ, for the sake of my brothers and sisters, my kinsfolk according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They are Israelites; theirs are the adoption and the glory and the covenants and the giving of the Law and the worship and the promises;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: theirs are the fathers, and from them comes the Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor are they all children because they are Abraham’s offspring; rather,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Through Isaac your offspring will be called.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the word of promise was this:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “About this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only that, but there was also Rebecca, who conceived children by one man, our father Isaac.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or bad—so that God’s purpose according to his choice might stand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not by works but by the one who calls—she was told,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The older will serve the younger,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he says to Moses,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I have compassion.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, it depends not on the one who wants or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might display my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, he has mercy on whomever he wants, and he hardens whomever he wants.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You will say to me then,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why then does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But who indeed are you, a human being, to talk back to God? Will the thing molded say to the one who molded it,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why did you make me like this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And what if God, wanting to display his wrath and to make known his power, bore with great patience vessels of wrath made ready for destruction,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and did so in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: namely us, whom he also called, not only from among Jews but also from among Gentiles?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he also says in Hosea,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will call those who are not my people ‘my people,’ and her who is not loved ‘loved.’”

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, it is the remnant that will be saved;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as Isaiah said beforehand,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “If the Lord of Hosts had not left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, laid hold of righteousness—the righteousness that is by faith;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not reach that law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Why? Because they pursued it not by faith but as if by works. They stumbled over the stone of stumbling,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “See, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock that makes people fall, and the one who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

notes.note: The Greek word, anathema, is the Septuagint’s term for something handed over to God for destruction and so placed under a curse. The Greek says literally “accursed from Christ”; “cut off” is supplied to make the phrase work in English. The verb “I could wish” is in a past tense that here expresses a wish the speaker knows cannot be granted, and many interpreters hear an echo of Moses’ offer in Exodus 32:32.

notes.phrase: who is over all, God blessed forever
notes.traditional: who is over all, God blessed for ever
notes.note: The earliest Greek manuscripts have little or no punctuation, and this clause can be read in two ways. Taken with what precedes, as here and in most English versions, it calls Christ “God blessed forever”; with a full stop after “flesh” it becomes a separate doxology, “God who is over all be blessed forever.” The word order favors the first reading, since Paul’s independent doxologies are phrased differently, but a number of scholars and translations prefer the second because Paul rarely if ever calls Christ “God” outright elsewhere.

The traditional word is “election,” which today suggests voting or a technical term of theology. The Greek noun is the ordinary word for a choice or selection, and the phrase describes God’s purpose as one that works by his choosing. The sense is not disputed; most versions keep “election” or write “God’s purpose in election.”

The quotation is Malachi 1:2–3, where Jacob and Esau stand for the nations descended from them, Israel and Edom. In biblical idiom “love” and “hate” set side by side can express choosing one over another and not only emotion (compare Genesis 29:30–31; Luke 14:26). Interpreters differ on how far that softens the statement here.

The Greek participle can give a reason (“because he wanted to display his wrath”) or a concession (“although he wanted to display his wrath, he held back”). The translation leaves this open, as the Greek does. The sentence running through verse 24 is also grammatically incomplete, an “if” with no “then,” which English conveys with “what if.”

The Greek does not say who did the preparing. It can be read as “prepared” by God, as “having made themselves ready,” or simply as a description, “ripe for destruction.” Many point out that for the vessels of mercy in the next verse Paul uses a different, active verb with God as its subject; others hold that God is the implied agent in both.

Greek has a single word, ethnos, for a nation and, in the plural, for the non-Jewish peoples, where English uses both “nations” and “Gentiles.” Here and in verse 30 the contrast with Jews and with Israel shows that the second sense is meant.

notes.phrase: completing it and cutting it short
notes.traditional: he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have this short form of the quotation from Isaiah 10:22–23. Later manuscripts fill it out from the Greek Old Testament, which is the form the King James Version translates. The meaning of the two participles is itself debated; the likely sense is that the Lord will carry out his sentence completely and without delay.

Paul, following the Greek version of Isaiah 1:9, leaves the Hebrew word untranslated: “Lord Sabaoth.” It means “of armies,” usually understood as the heavenly forces at God’s command. “Hosts” is the long-established English rendering and is an old word for armies.

Greek uses one word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice.” The “injustice” denied of God in verse 14 is the negative of the word translated “righteousness” here. Some scholars prefer “justice” throughout; “righteousness” is kept because “justice” tends to suggest punishment to a modern reader.

notes.phrase: a rock that makes people fall
notes.note: The quotation joins two passages of Isaiah: the stone laid in Zion from 28:16, and the stone of stumbling and rock of falling from 8:14. Older versions have “rock of offence,” but the Greek word means something that trips a person up, not something that hurts feelings. “In him” could also be translated “in it,” meaning the stone; Paul applies the stone to Christ, as 10:11 shows.

candidates.reason: The plural recurs throughout the letters for mixed groups (here for fellow Jews), and versions split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and paraphrases, so one policy is needed.

Paul’s uses range from physical descent (as here) to the sinful human condition, and translations vary between “flesh,” “human descent,” “sinful nature” and others; readers need to see when it is the same word.

The collective singular for descendants drives arguments here and in Galatians 3:16, and “seed,” “offspring” and “descendants” all appear in English versions; the choice must match across those passages.
“Election” is traditional but now reads as political or technical; the noun and its relatives (ἐκλεκτός, ἐκλέγομαι) recur in Romans 11, 1 Thessalonians and 2 Peter and need a uniform decision.
A transliterated Hebrew title occurring only here and in James 5:4; “hosts” is archaic, “armies” and “Almighty” are rivals, and it may qualify for retention as “Sabaoth” under the loanword rule.
